The relationship between human reading durations and linguistic surprise, as measured by language models, has been extensively researched. However, recent studies have found significant discrepancies between human and state-of-the-art language model predictions on reading duration. This study investigates whether these predictions from high-capacity transformer models are inherently flawed or if improvements in model design could rectify the issue. We found that higher model accuracy is not directly correlated with reduced prediction errors, suggesting that these models are inherently flawed. We discovered that these errors stem from two issues: first, state-of-the-art models tend to overestimate the significance of specific words, leading to larger prediction errors; second, these models struggle with infrequent words, resulting in increased errors. We proposed a new approach called sparse attention, which reduces model overfitting and improves prediction accuracy. We successfully applied this approach to various language models, significantly reducing the discrepancy between human and model-based predictions on reading duration. This study provides valuable insights into the limitations of current language models and offers a potential solution to improve their performance in modeling human reading behavior. The escalating scale of botnet threats has prompted the development of countermeasures to detect and mitigate these attacks. This research employs Command Data Messages (CDM) obtained from honeypots to identify botnet groups. Historically, analyzing CDM has been challenging due to the lack of effective analytical techniques. This study leverages Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to extract meaningful information from CDM from honeypots. Specifically, we utilize bag-of-words models, along with statistical and machine learning methods, to identify botnet groups. Our research demonstrates that machine learning algorithms can be successfully applied to CDM to identify these groups. We also propose a novel method for generating candidate commands that are likely to be part of a botnet, based on the frequency of related commands in the data. This approach enables us to identify botnet members without requiring prior knowledge of the group's commands. Our evaluation of the method on a dataset of 1,000 machine learning models trained on 1,000,000 CDMs yields promising results. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of this method to identify botnet members without requiring prior knowledge of the group's commands. Our research contributes to the body of knowledge by introducing a new technique for identifying botnet members and analyzing command logs. This technique can be used in conjunction with other methods, such as the botnet graph model, to further enhance botnet detection capabilities. This study is the first to explore the use of NLP to identify botnet members, and its findings can be applied in real-world scenarios to detect and mitigate botnet attacks. Brain tumor segmentation using MRI scans is a crucial step in developing effective treatment plans. The challenge lies in accurately segmenting tumors from the brain, as it is a highly complex task. To address this issue, we propose a novel 3D U-Net-based approach that incorporates contextual information. The approach uses a 3D U-Net to extract tumor features and a 2D CNN to incorporate contextual information. The contextual information is then fed into a 1x1 convolutional layer to generate a probability map. This map is then combined with the UNet features to produce a final segmentation map. To further improve performance, we also incorporate a conditional variance-based skip connection. Our approach was evaluated on the BRATS 2019 dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to other methods. Notably, the use of contextual information resulted in significant improvements, particularly in the tumor core and enhancement segments. The source code for our approach is available on GitHub for public use. Further, we plan to enhance our approach by leveraging attention mechanisms to extract more informative features. The ultimate goal of our research is to develop a robust brain tumor segmentation model that can be seamlessly integrated into clinical settings. Temporal modeling of videos is hindered by the massive storage and computational requirements that come with large-scale video data. To overcome this, we present a new framework called Gradient Forward-Transmission (GF-T) that efficiently processes video content. This framework involves dividing videos into segments, using a teacher model to generate initial representations, and then fine-tuning the representations with a smaller student model. The student model's parameters are updated in real-time using the teacher's gradients, allowing for a reduced video stream. Our experimental results show that GF-T outperforms existing methods, achieving a significant improvement of 3.4% top-1 accuracy on the HowTo100M dataset. Moreover, we introduce a new task called video domain generalization, where we evaluate our model's ability to perform well on unseen domains despite being trained on limited data. Our experiments demonstrate that GF-T achieves state-of-the-art results on this new task, even when trained with only 10% of the data. Our code will be publicly available for further research. This paper introduces a unique, efficiently computable matrix where each row shares the same pattern, consisting of distinct groups of entries. By leveraging the property that the permanent remains unchanged when rearranging the rows and columns, we can efficiently calculate the permanent of this specific matrix through recursive formulas, bypassing the need for any permutations. This approach offers significant computational advantages over the standard method for calculating permanents. Additionally, we establish a connection between the permanent of this matrix and a particular type of polynomial. Our findings also extend to a more general case involving matrices with circulant structures that can be grouped into rows and columns. Furthermore, we develop a new, efficient algorithm to calculate the permanent of these circulant matrices. This algorithm, based on the property of circulant matrices allowing for efficient multiplication, offers a linear-time complexity in contrast to the existing Brualdi and Hwang algorithm. Finally, we explore the applicability of our methods to a broader range of problems and discuss their significance in combinatorial number theory. A crucial component of visual navigation in autonomous vehicles is the loop closure detection and localization function. This function enables robots to identify and pinpoint their position within a previously mapped area, thereby preventing the accumulation of positioning errors that occur when relying solely on dead reckoning. The majority of existing loop closure detection and localization algorithms rely on a one-way search approach, which can be inefficient in real-world applications where large maps lead to lengthy search times. This paper presents a dual-path approach that accelerates the search process by concurrently searching within the map and from the map's origin to the corresponding location in real-time. The dual-path approach is demonstrated to significantly enhance a SLAM system's performance by conducting experiments on a KITTI dataset, which show that it can achieve a 2-4 times faster search process with comparable precision rates. The dual-path approach is achieved by integrating a bidirectional search method with a SLAM system that utilizes a monocular visual-inertial tracker. The paper further presents a novel feature descriptor named FPF (Feature Pyramid Pyramid Feature), which combines pyramid pyramid features to enhance the accuracy of feature matching and demonstrates its superiority over existing descriptors in challenging scenarios. The dual-path approach and FPF descriptor are integrated into a SLAM system and evaluated on a KITTI dataset, with results showing a significant improvement in feature matching accuracy. A quantum translator is a specific quantum sub-circuit that translates the basis of a quantum circuit's input into the basis of its output. However, current quantum translators have limitations because they cannot simultaneously convert multiple qubits to different bases while preserving the other qubits in their original form. This paper introduces new quantum translators that improve upon existing designs. The new translators can convert multiple qubits to different bases simultaneously, which increases their potential applications. Specifically, these new quantum translators can convert qubits to the Gell-Mann basis, a basis used in the computation of certain multi-qubit quantum operations. The paper also presents a new quantum translator that converts a qubit from the standard basis to the Gell-Mann basis. This new quantum translator has the potential to speed up certain quantum translators and also facilitates the computation of certain multi-qubit quantum operations. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new quantum translator that converts a qubit from the standard basis to the Bell basis, and another that converts a qubit from the standard basis to the Hadamard basis. These new quantum translators can be used to speed up certain quantum operations such as the controlled-swap gate and the Toffoli gate. The paper also presents a new quantum translator that converts qubits to the standard basis from any other basis, which is useful for resolving the measurement collapse issue in quantum computing. Overall, the new quantum translators have the potential to increase the efficiency of quantum operations and make quantum computing more practical. This paper is an extension of the authors' previous work that was presented at the 2022 International Conference on Computational Intelligence and Hardware (ICHI-CI'22). The new quantum translators have been implemented in the IBM Qiskit software framework, and their performance has been tested on a 5-qubit IBM Q simulator. Cache side-channel attacks have been identified as a threat to software security, 
allowing attackers to extract sensitive information by analyzing cache collisions. 
While recent research has developed methods to detect and mitigate these attacks, 
a key challenge remains in understanding the underlying causes of cache side-channel vulnerabilities. 

To address this challenge, we introduce CacheQL, a novel tool for measuring 
cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software. CacheQL leverages a unique 
approach that combines a cache-unsafe programming model with a robust profiling 
and monitoring system to accurately quantify cache side-channel weaknesses in 
affected applications. 

We demonstrate the effectiveness of CacheQL in assessing the cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in popular third-party libraries, specifically in QEMU, Nettle, and 
LibGCompr. Our results show that QEMU and Nettle suffer from cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities, while LibGCompr has significant vulnerabilities in its CPU and 
memory access components. 

We also propose a method to localize the root causes of cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in software, which we demonstrate in our analysis of LibGCompr, 
identifying a specific instruction set and cache line combination that causes 
vulnerabilities. 

Our research highlights the practical value of CacheQL in assessing cache side-channel 
vulnerabilities in production software, providing a new tool for developers and 
security auditors to accurately measure and localize these threats. 

We make CacheQL source code publicly available for research and development 
purposes, and invite researchers to contribute to its development. 

Our study also reveals that while existing software mitigations, such as cache 
bypassing and randomization, can reduce cache side-channel attacks, they do not 
eliminate the underlying vulnerabilities. 

Our research findings suggest that a combination of software design and development 
practices is necessary to prevent and detect cache side-channel attacks. 

We make a call to action for software developers and security auditors to adopt 
this research and work together to address the cache side-channel threat, 
providing a more secure and reliable software stack for the future. 

Our research findings and the CacheQL tool are available at 
https://github.com/UCeFT/CacheQL. 

We also present our research at the USENIX Security 2021 conference.

Additionally, the researchers adapt the two-sided Lanczos method to develop a low-rank, constraint-preconditioned CG algorithm, resulting in a memory-efficient and robust method for solving constrained saddle-point systems. This research also explores the use of the proposed methods for solving linear complementarity problems, a common problem class arising in various applications. Overall, the proposed methods demonstrate high performance and robustness in solving regularized saddle-position systems and linear complementarity problems. Furthermore, the researchers provide open-source implementations of the proposed methods in the ALBERT package, accessible at https://github.com/colsony/ALBERT. This package includes Python implementations of the proposed methods, as well as various test problems and benchmarks for evaluation. In addition, the researchers provide a comparison of the proposed methods with other popular CG algorithms for solving constrained saddle-point systems. This comparison is based on the same preconditioner and solver, with the results indicating that the proposed methods outperform the other algorithms in most cases, highlighting the efficiency and robustness of the proposed methods. In conclusion, the proposed methods demonstrate the ability to solve complex saddle-position systems and linear complementarity problems efficiently and robustly, making them a valuable resource for researchers in this field. A new pre-mature termination criterion for the GMRES algorithm used in the IP method to solve symmetric positive definite linear systems is proposed. This criterion relies on the relationship between early termination and the residual norm being less than the product of the smallest and largest eigenvalue of the system's matrix multiplied by the norm of the error. By computing this product at the initial step, the need for recurrent computation during Krylov methods is avoided. A comparison with a widely used, but unstable, termination criterion based on residual growth is shown through numerical experiments, demonstrating the new criterion's stability and potential to reduce computational costs. Additionally, the potential for early termination of other Krylov methods, such as GMRES, CG, and MINRES, is explored. However, results indicate that while early termination is possible, it is not consistently more beneficial than using GMRES with the proposed termination criterion. This is likely due to GMRES's ability to provide accurate results in subsequent IP method iterations. As a result, our proposed termination criterion is recommended for implementation within Krylov methods. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where PT symmetry breaks down, resulting in eigenvalues with zero or infinite imaginary components, and we discuss the implications of these findings for the study of quantum paths in interaction with an external electromagnetic field. Specifically, we analyze the scenario of a charged particle approaching a heavy, complex nucleus. A novel approach to extracting key features from time series data is introduced, involving the application of a dynamic filter to isolate the system's dynamics from noise. This methodology is demonstrated through the use of Lyapunov and correlation spectra, as well as the autocorrelation function, all of which are computationally efficient and resilient to noise. A key aspect of this technique lies in its ability to distinguish the system's dynamics from noise by testing its sensitivity to input. Furthermore, it can be employed to filter out unwanted information while preserving the system's essential characteristics. This methodology is validated through the analysis of two distinct systems: a chaotic model and a real-world benchmark. This benchmark, comprised of the S-6 dataset, is derived from the NARMAX representation of the solar system, a complex time series problem that poses a significant challenge for identification and control. The results indicate that the proposed approach yields results comparable to existing literature while requiring significantly less than 1% of the computational resources. This methodology is anticipated to have far-reaching applications in the field of time series analysis, particularly in the domains of system identification, control, and optimization. A novel unsupervised clustering approach called the "Weighted Density Ratio Clustering" (WDC) method has been developed to find compact clusters in high-dimensional data while maintaining interpretability. The first stage maximizes the intra-cluster density, whereas the second stage minimizes the variance between clusters. To achieve this, WDC utilizes a weighted density ratio approach that estimates the density of samples and assigns weights to data points based on their distances to cluster centroids. The method then identifies the most significant clusters by maximizing the weighted log-likelihood of the data. The optimization problem is solved using the gradient descent algorithm, resulting in the identification of the most significant clusters. The spread of misinformation can have far-reaching consequences on individuals and society as a whole. Despite this, prior research on combating misinformation has been hampered by the lack of a comprehensive definition and a robust evaluation framework. Furthermore, existing methods for detecting misinformation are often ineffective due to the limitations of standard evaluation datasets. In an effort to address this issue, we introduce a new framework for evaluating propaganda-laden text, which involves creating training data that incorporates real news articles, artificially generated false news, and propaganda-rich articles. We also develop a new model, Falsifying False News, which leverages this dataset to improve false news detection. Our proposed framework and model demonstrate significant gains in detecting propaganda, detecting false news, and distinguishing between propaganda and false news. Moreover, we release our dataset and code publicly to facilitate further research in this area. The key contributions of our work are threefold: (1) we introduce a new definition of propaganda and a corresponding evaluation framework; (2) we develop a novel method for creating training data that incorporates propaganda; (3) we introduce a new model for detecting false news, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Unlike conventional steganography methods that adjust one image many times, SABMIS optimizes a single image to minimize changes and maintain its quality. To embed the hidden information, SABMIS uses a modified sparse estimation approach that adjusts the pixels of the target image. Once the hidden message is extracted, the receiver resolves a similar sparse representation problem to retrieve the data. Our simulations demonstrate that SABMIS achieves higher security and efficiency than competing techniques. We derive this result by first establishing a corresponding result for a related model, known as the q-gamma random walk. A novel approach to disease surveillance has been developed using digital syndromic data, which can identify emerging health threats earlier than traditional methods. A study of this approach, referred to as Generalized Syndromic Monitoring (GSM), has been re-examined. GSM involves creating a statistical model for each disease stage, which is then updated regularly using current syndromic data. A threshold is set for each model based on historical data trends, and any deviation from this threshold is considered a potential outbreak. The study's findings suggest that GSM can be an effective tool for monitoring infectious diseases and identifying potential outbreaks, and its potential applications should be explored in further research. The task of evaluating text-based emotions is complicated by the subjective nature of emotions themselves as well as the influence of external factors, including preconceived notions and manipulation attempts, on how people perceive and express emotions. Although studies have explored the impact of knowledge about speakers on sentiment analysis, the potential for explicit manipulation of emotions remains largely unexplored. This study delves into the effects of guiding people to express their emotions through verbal feedback. Specifically, we examine how inducing individuals to recall a particular type of experience affects their sentiment analysis ratings. In our experiment, participants were asked to recall either a positive or a neutral event while reading a news article and provide annotations for sentiment. Our findings reveal that when individuals recall a positive event, they tend to mark more positive comments as correct, even if the text actually expresses negative sentiments. This observation aligns with prior research highlighting the impact of personal feelings on interpreting emotions. Our study sheds light on the underlying psychological mechanisms influencing sentiment analysis and offers insights into how to account for these biases in sentiment analysis systems. The implications of our findings suggest that integrating knowledge about speakers' emotions into sentiment analysis models may be a crucial step toward creating more accurate systems. This could be achieved by incorporating a representation of the speaker's emotional state, such as a "emotion embedding", into the sentiment analysis model. However, they are susceptible to overfitting due to their limited ability to focus on distant graph regions. We propose a novel framework that integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with model-based control, leveraging the active inference framework. This approach, termed RLAI, formulates action selection as maximizing the likelihood of anticipated sensory outcomes. By doing so, RLAI unifies RL and expectation maximization (EM) algorithms, allowing for a broader information-theoretic foundation. Moreover, RLAI bypasses the need for reward-based optimization and instead directly optimizes a performance metric, making it more suitable for real-world applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RLAI on both theoretical and practical tasks, including a robotic arm control scenario, and highlight its potential advantages over traditional RL methods. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that RLAI can be viewed as a variational inference problem, where the goal is to find an optimal policy that minimizes the difference between the model's predicted and true posterior distributions. This perspective offers a more comprehensive understanding of RL and highlights the potential for future research in the field. In today's digital landscape, social media has become a primary source for information and intellectual enrichment. However, its influence extends further, shaping users' perceptions of reality, news, and opinions on significant issues. This study explores the impact of social media on belief formation, with a particular focus on how users' true beliefs are shaped by the information they consume online. We develop a theoretical framework that explains individuals' belief development as a process influenced by information consumption, social connections, and the desire to present oneself in a favorable light. By combining this framework with publicly available data from Twitter, we demonstrate that people's true beliefs are distorted by the influence of misinformation, social manipulation, and the desire to project a positive image. Specifically, we show that the spread of misinformation can significantly alter people's opinions and that individuals tend to present themselves in a more favorable light than their actual beliefs would suggest. This research offers a novel perspective on the role of social media in shaping beliefs, highlighting the potential consequences of social media's influence on belief formation. Moreover, our findings provide valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and individuals who engage with social media platforms. By understanding the mechanisms at play in the formation of beliefs, we can better comprehend the importance of maintaining an open mind, cultivating critical thinking skills, and being aware of the potential for misinformation and social manipulation within our online communities. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of social media in shaping our beliefs, with the ultimate goal of promoting greater intellectual curiosity and a more nuanced understanding of the world. We investigate how different methods for grouping galaxies and analyzing their patterns affect the results, and we use a simulated universe to compare various approaches. We find that using a specific type of galaxy grouping method called friends-of-friends finds the most massive groups and produces the fewest systematic errors, but it is less efficient than other methods. We also find that using the halo occupation distribution to model galaxy distribution produces more accurate results than other models, and it can significantly reduce systematic errors. We use these methods to analyze a real dataset of galaxies, and we find that our results agree with previous studies on the growth of the universe, but with some discrepancies. We also find that using the halo occupation distribution to model galaxy distribution produces fewer systematic errors than other models. Overall, our results suggest that galaxy groupings can be a useful tool for cosmological research, but with some limitations and depending on how they are analyzed. To demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness, it is applied to a specific problem: the resummation of the Clausen hyperelliptic integral of the second kind. This study investigates the optical properties of carbon dots generated from cigarette smoke and explores their potential application in bio-imaging. The carbon dots, measuring around 3 nm in size, exhibit photoluminescence properties at low temperatures. The source of this luminescence is attributed to the coupling of localized surface plasmons and a tightly bound pair of electrons in a spin-singlet state. The study also examines the cellular uptake of these carbon dots in living cells. The combination of these properties makes these carbon dots suitable for use in bio-imaging applications. Furthermore, this research offers a novel approach for converting cigarette smoke, a common waste product, into a valuable resource for bio-imaging and other potential uses. The carbon dots, derived from cigarette smoke, can be used to develop innovative bio-imaging agents. Additionally, this research highlights the potential of cigarette smoke as a precursor for creating various types of carbon-based materials. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the optical properties of carbon dots and their potential use in bio-imaging. The development of carbon-based materials from cigarette smoke could also lead to significant economic benefits. Ultimately, this research aims to inspire further investigation into the properties and applications of carbon dots and other types of carbon-based materials. The authors also aim to promote the use of cigarette smoke as a precursor in the production of carbon-based materials. This paper introduces a new approach to 3D point cloud processing, utilizing deep learning with para-unitary representations. By leveraging the property of Euclidean invariance, para-unitary transformations can effectively capture the geometric structure of 3D data, and have been shown to be more efficient than graph convolutions in many cases. Additionally, the proposed para-unitary network (ParaNet) can learn geometric relationships without the need for additional supervision, outperforming graph convolutions in many tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that ParaNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in various 3D point cloud processing tasks, including classification, upsampling, and novel view synthesis. Further analysis reveals that ParaNet's ability to learn local geometric context is a key factor in its success. With the potential for significant impact, the research presented in this paper is expected to benefit a wide range of 3D point cloud processing applications. This involves applying a simple method to transform these equations into a standard form and presenting the resulting solutions in both graphic and analytical form. Due to the versatility of the proposed methods, they can be applied to a broad spectrum of nonlinear fractional models that have not been extensively studied in the existing literature. Illustrative examples demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed techniques, which yield exact solutions for equations like the fractional nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, the fractional nonlinear heat equation, the fractional nonlinear diffusion equation, the fractional Kadomtsev--Petviashvili equation, the fractional Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation, the fractional Dullundur equation, as well as the three-dimensional nonlinear wave equation. These solutions encompass solitons, Jacobi elliptic periodic waves, and Weierstrass elliptic periodic waves. It is anticipated that the presented solutions will serve as valuable benchmarks for testing numerical algorithms aimed at solving fractional differential equations in the future. All the obtained results have been verified using the Mathematica software package. In addition, the proposed methods can be easily adapted to study other types of fractional equations, such as those involving the Caputo derivative. A gradient-based optimization approach is developed to estimate the geometric convergence rate of preconditioned eigensolvers. By reformulating the geometric convergence target functional, the method addresses difficulties in its non-differentiability at zero eigenvalues and introduces a computational reproducibility verification process. Numerical experiments validate the method's effectiveness for both perfectly and imperfect preconditioners. Additionally, the method is capable of measuring geometric convergence for any eigenvalue, not just the first one, and is applicable to various eigensolver classes, including iterative and template-based solvers. Its flexibility is further demonstrated by its ability to measure geometric convergence in both pre- and post-processing stages. Furthermore, the method is also used to optimize geometric convergence in pre-conditioned eigensolvers. The results are then utilized to improve the geometric convergence of a pre-conditioned Arnoldi method. The developed approach is also applicable to solving linear systems through iterative solvers. Overall, the method provides a simple, efficient, and universally applicable framework for assessing geometric convergence. Its source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/JulienFehrenbach/Precond-convergence. The collapse of protostellar clouds is a crucial phase in star formation, significantly influenced by magnetic fields. Researchers have conducted a series of simulations using the Enzo code to examine the collapse of non-spinning and spinning magnetic clouds, revealing that magnetic fields play a less prominent role in star formation than previously thought. Their findings indicate that protostellar clouds collapse under the influence of thermal pressure, with magnetic fields exerting their greatest force outside the innermost regions of the protostar. Additionally, the collapse of protostellar clouds is found to be highly sensitive to the strength of the magnetic field connecting the protostar to the surrounding material. When the magnetic fields are strong, the collapse of the material is significantly slowed, resulting in the formation of a long, narrow jet of material that is ejected at high speeds. On the other hand, the collapse of protostellar clouds with weaker magnetic fields leads to the formation of a disk-like structure, with a relatively short outflow channel that produces material that is ejected at moderate speeds. Researchers have identified a critical threshold in the strength of the magnetic field that determines whether a narrow or wide jet forms during protostellar collapse, with a value of approximately 10^3 Gauss. Their results suggest that protostellar clouds may exhibit a range of morphologies, with a strong or weak jet, depending on the strength of their magnetic fields. These findings have significant implications for understanding the collapse of protostellar clouds, particularly in the context of low-mass stars. This approach enables a deeper understanding of Lenia's rule space and its potential for generating a wide range of interesting patterns. By comparing Lenia's rules to those of the Game of Life, the authors aim to shed new light on the role of mass conservation in creating life-like behaviors. The evaluation of researchers' influence has become a critical consideration, primarily due to the difficulty in quantifying its various aspects. We present a comprehensive model to assess the impact of authors through a system-level approach, distinct from traditional individual-focused methods. This approach considers personal characteristics, including expertise and collaboration patterns, to provide an objective assessment of a researcher's contribution. Furthermore, it allows for the evaluation of various collaboration strategies and informs policy decisions in research and scientific communities. The proposed method can be integrated with existing citation metrics to gain insights into the effects of personal characteristics and collaboration strategies on research output. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using a large dataset of publications from Scopus, covering multiple disciplines. The results suggest that, while personal characteristics and collaboration strategies have a limited impact on research output, their influence can be amplified through specific strategies such as joining established research groups or initiating and succeeding as their leaders. The findings also highlight the underestimation of authors' influence by citation metrics and the need for a more balanced approach that incorporates these metrics. Our research framework offers a practical tool for researchers, policymakers, and research leaders to assess and improve collaboration and research outcomes. We introduce Entailer, a large-scale model designed to generate conversational
responses through step-by-step reasoning. When answering a question, Entailer crafts a series of intermediate steps and uses its extensive knowledge base to determine plausible responses. This approach allows for the establishment of fact-based chains of reasoning, making it an effective tool for transparent and reliable human communication. To train Entailer, we adapt the GPT3 model through a novel self-supervised method that incorporates a new type of input: multi-hop queries. This modified model can generate responses in two formats: plain text and structured reasoning trees, enabling seamless human evaluation. Through self-supervised learning, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in complex question-answering tasks, outperforming comparable models that rely on additional supervision. Additionally, Entailer's responses are found to be more accurate and its generated chains of reasoning are more accurately reflected in the original human-written answers. When evaluated with a new dataset of multi-hop reasoning tasks, both human and automated assessments confirm that Entailer's responses are more accurate and its generated chains of reasoning are more faithful compared to other models. To further enhance transparency, Entailer's responses are visualized as parsed trees, illustrating the intermediate reasoning steps and source evidence in the form of annotated fact graphs. This representation allows for a deeper understanding of the model's reasoning process and facilitates the creation of more accurate and reliable human communication. These findings highlight the importance of considering the influence of trading on grid frequency stability and suggest that specific market factors can either exacerbate or mitigate this effect. As the energy transition accelerates, it is crucial to develop a comprehensive understanding of the impact of trading on grid frequency stability to ensure the resilience of power systems. In this research, we investigate a constrained Markov Decision Process where an agent's goal is to maximize long-term rewards while adhering to complex restrictions on states and actions. We focus on a scenario where the agent has limited access to the MDP's structure, must consider both constraints on states and actions, and can only rely on online data collection without any external assistance. To address this challenge, we developed a method that integrates constraint satisfaction into a policy optimization process using a technique called Proximal Policy Optimization. This approach effectively transforms the constraints into a penalty term within the objective function, allowing for a more efficient and scalable optimization process. Additionally, our method incorporates a data-efficient sampling strategy that ensures the satisfaction of all constraints at all times. Through a detailed convergence analysis, we demonstrate that our algorithm converges rapidly to a solution under specific conditions and show, via numerical experiments on a range of synthetic benchmarks, that our approach consistently outperforms existing policies and yields significantly faster convergence rates. Moreover, our method is capable of handling large and complex MDPs, resulting in substantial improvements in both efficiency and performance. Finally, we successfully applied our algorithm to a real-world problem, a robotic manipulation task, where the algorithm successfully optimized the policy to maximize rewards while maintaining contact with the environment, achieving a notable improvement in performance over existing methods. This paper resolves long-standing questions raised by Z. M\"enger} regarding spaces with specific geometric properties. Specifically, we address his 1930 questions about whether certain geometric spaces are homeomorphic to each other, and whether a specific type of metric space with large angles contains a simpler metric space with larger angles. Z., 37:170-205}, as well as in M\"enger's 1932 paper "Geometrie und Metrik",  Encyklop\"edeie der mathematischen Wissenschaften. We provide answers to these questions and explore related properties of spaces with large angles. We also offer a simplified proof of a major theorem regarding these spaces, originally proved by R. Lavery in 1987. Finally, we examine some unresolved problems associated with M\"enger's work on angle spaces. This research introduces a novel approach for cooperative speed control in multi-lane scenarios with passing vehicles, utilizing a random model predictive predictive controller based on Gaussian Process (GPs). By leveraging GP regression, the controller estimates passing vehicle speeds as random variables, enabling the random model predictive predictive controller to optimize longitudinal velocity profiles for all vehicles. The resulting velocity profiles ensure safe gaps and headings between vehicles, and natural passing motions are facilitated. The proposed controller's efficacy is validated through comparative simulations. The results show that the random model predictive predictive controller outperforms its deterministic counterpart in terms of tracking performance, particularly during passing maneuvers, and is capable of handling model uncertainties. Additionally, the controller's computational efficiency is demonstrated, enabling real-time control execution. During the Covid-19 pandemic, emergency medical services experienced a surge in calls. As the virus spread, people delayed seeking care for non-Covid health issues, leading to a rise in acute conditions that needed emergency medical service attention. To address this issue, we created a forecasting model that predicts the number of EMS calls for non-Covid conditions and capacity issues. Our analysis of daily EMS calls from New York City from March to November 2019 found that Covid-19 had a profound impact on healthcare demand. We then used our findings to develop a predictive model that can estimate future EMS demand. Our results show that failing to address this increase in healthcare need could lead to critical hospital capacity issues. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our study and potential avenues for future research. This paper explores the behavior of a two-dimensional non-isothermal chemotactic model with logistic growth and a specific sensitivity relationship. This model is based on a set of nonlinear partial differential equations describing the movement and reproduction of a biological species influenced by chemical signals and temperature. We establish that if the signal diffusion rate is sufficiently high, there will be a specific solution to this model that exists globally in time. Moreover, we demonstrate the asymptotic stability of a constant solution under certain conditions. Our findings are derived using the combination of various mathematical techniques, including estimates of temperature and signal concentrations, a specific model based on a Poincaré inequality, and a finite-dimensional reduction method. This research builds upon previous studies of related models and contributes to a deeper understanding of their long-term behavior. As such, it contributes to a broader theoretical framework for modeling complex biological systems. This work has been submitted for publication in the journal Mathematical Biosciences and Applications (MBA). The manuscript is currently undergoing a thorough review process prior to publication. Ultimately, this research is intended to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics at play in biological systems and inform the development of more effective mathematical models for predicting their behavior. The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming into a vast network of interconnected devices, generating vast amounts of data from various sources, which is then analyzed to provide insights for data owners. However, this process is often done centrally by cloud servers, which raises privacy and security concerns. A more decentralized approach, where data is processed locally, offers a solution but is often limited by devices' computational capabilities. To overcome these challenges, offloading computations to cloud data centers has become a viable option, yet often leads to issues with slow response times and security concerns. To address these problems, we propose Self-Managed IoT (SMIoT), a novel framework that allows users to offload computations to multiple cloud data centers, ensuring efficient resource allocation and minimizing response time variations. By implementing a two-level auction mechanism, SMIoT incentivizes data centers to provide high-quality services while maintaining users' costs in check. To further optimize performance, SMIoT incorporates a machine learning-based offloading decision algorithm that takes into account users' needs and data characteristics. Through extensive simulations, SMIoT has demonstrated its ability to provide superior performance, achieving an 80% average offloading rate and a 90% average reduction in response time across various scenarios. Additionally, SMIoT has been successfully implemented in a real-world IoT testbed, showcasing its feasibility and benefits in practical applications. However, implementing these networks is a complex task due to the need for backpropagation through time, which can be computationally demanding.  To address this issue, researchers have employed surrogate gradients as a solution, but these networks often struggle with convergence when using this method.  To address this problem, we introduce a novel approach that combines weight regularization and input standardization to enhance the performance of surrogate gradient-based spiking neural networks.  Through extensive testing on various classification tasks, we have found that these methods consistently lead to better results, and in some cases, even outperform conventional backpropagation methods.  In particular, our approach has resulted in improved accuracy of up to 5% and reduced training times of up to 20% on complex image classification tasks.  Additionally, our findings demonstrate that our method can handle large datasets more efficiently, and with reduced memory requirements.  Overall, our research highlights the benefits of using regularization and standardization in the development of efficient and accurate spiking neural networks. In software engineering, researchers often use traceability analysis to study connections between development artifacts like source codes and requirements.  However, a major challenge is extracting reliable mappings between these artifacts.  To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages pre-trained language models to enhance semi-automated traceability analysis by pinpointing exact text segments within code snippets that refer to specific requirements. This approach outperforms existing methods according to evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, f-measure, and total Hamming distance.  Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of pre-trained language models reveals that BERT-based models yield more accurate results.  Additionally, a tool called BERT-Mapper has been created to facilitate reproducibility and practical application of this research.  The tool is available at a publicly accessible repository.  Experimental results and the tool's repository can be accessed at https://github.com/abdurrahmanabualwua/bert-mapper.  The data used for this research is available at https://github.com/berkaygulmez/traceability-analysis.

This paper introduces a novel decentralized architecture for control systems that enables distributed control and analysis over networks, relying on a technique called multi-channel regulation. Key constraints are identified, and a corresponding problem is defined and analyzed. Building on this, a practical approach is developed for solving the problem in a distributed and modular manner. Central to this approach is a new algorithm that facilitates communication among control channels. Results from numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Specifically, the simulations show that the proposed method can achieve stable control even in systems with unstable components, and that the distribution of workload can be more evenly spread when different parts of the system are controlled by multiple channels. These findings are further validated by an experimental demonstration using a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle. Ultimately, the proposed method is shown to offer a flexible, scalable, and reliable control solution suitable for use across a wide range of applications. To assess whether this strategy is effective, we can learn from it by analyzing how a language model incorporates categories of entities to streamline the writing process. This allowed us to investigate how models trained with the help of annotated entities (known as E-Grounded) perform in producing text that incorporates specific categories of entities. Our results show that models trained with entity guidance tend to use categories of entities to create coherent text that is less repetitive. Additionally, we observed that the categories of entities used by the model tend to align with human guidance. This study provides a framework for understanding how categories of entities can be leveraged to enhance the writing process. Our work also highlights the potential for using categories of entities to improve the generation of specific types of text. Smart contracts are small programs deployed on blockchains like Ethereum to facilitate secure, decentralized interactions. Current approaches to writing these contracts in Solidity rely heavily on a central designer who must consider every possible use case. To overcome this limitation, we propose a tool that automatically generates Solidity code from specifications, even for complex scenarios with multiple parties and time-sensitive interactions. Our approach, based on a formal semantics of the Solidity language, utilizes a proof-based synthesis algorithm to produce valid, efficient, and minimal Solidity code from given specifications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our tool by applying it to several challenging problems, including authentication and confidentiality, with promising results. Furthermore, we highlight potential future research directions in applying formal methods to blockchain technology. The developed tool is available online for public use. https://smart-contract-synthesis.github.io/. The implementation is also accessible at https://github.com/ucsc-formal-methods/solidity-sem.

The development of highly accurate language models necessitates a substantial amount of high-quality training data. However, this process is hindered by the challenges of data collection, annotation, and curation. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have successfully employed pre-trained models and fine-tuning in a supervised or unsupervised capacity. This paper introduces an innovative approach to knowledge transfer, which enables models to learn from one another, reducing training costs and extending the lifespan of model checkpoints. Our method involves a two-stage process where the fine-tuned model from the previous stage serves as the knowledge source for further fine-tuning. We systematically examine the effects of different checkpoint sizes and fine-tuning stages on the final model's performance. Our results indicate that knowledge transfer not only reduces costs but also enhances model performance, particularly when combined with other techniques, such as data augmentation and ensemble methods. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the effects of different model sizes and fine-tuning stages on the final model's performance. Our findings are validated through experiments on three distinct datasets, which demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. We introduce a category of weak correlations with weaker conditions than Poissonian, defined through feeble Poissonian moments, which can be met under local measurements, even in non-informative situations. We demonstrate that any bipartite quantum state can be converted into a Poissonian state through local operations and entanglement, but achieving Poissonian entangement generally requires such preprocessing. We also discover that any system can produce feeble Poissonian correlations in a classical manner. This classification of correlations enables us to propose a new quantum task, called weak Poissonianity testing. We also explore the implications of feeble Poissonian correlations on quantum nonlocality, revealing that nonlocality is limited to weak forms, and develop a new understanding of nonlocality with Poissonianity as a special case. This work provides a framework for understanding correlations in quantum systems and their applications across various models. It also highlights the significance of distinguishing between different types of correlations in quantum information theory and its various applications. In the context of intent prediction, supervised learning methods often struggle to
account for real-world variability. To address this issue, we propose a novel
approach, called Witness Intent Prediction, which leverages a retrieval-based
framework. This method enables models to incorporate contextual information and
learn from diverse examples, even those outside the initial training set. To
further enhance the models' intent detection capabilities, we introduce the
Sample-Guided Intent Prediction task, which involves training models on a selected
subset of samples to improve performance on the remainder of the dataset. We
evaluate our approach through comprehensive experiments on two benchmark
datasets, achieving competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods. 
Our research also highlights the effectiveness of our sample-guided training
approach, demonstrating its potential to boost intent prediction accuracy. 
Moreover, we examine the potential pitfalls of our approach and suggest
strategies to optimize its performance. Our code and related resources are
available at the following repository: https://github.com/ylYang/SPiW. 
Future research may explore the application of our witness intent model across
different domains and tasks, such as named entity recognition and machine
translation.

Additionally, we provide access to our source code, data sets, and evaluation results to enable others to build upon our findings. Moreover, we present a visual game simulator that allows human players to compete against our AI model. Our study also includes a comparative analysis of the performance of different AI models, including Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Convolutional Q-Networks (CQN), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and identify areas for potential improvement. Ultimately, we identify the limitations of the current study and propose avenues for future investigation. Our research is a pioneering effort in exploring AI solutions for Tetris-Connection, and our approach can be adapted to other puzzles and games. This study introduces Distributed Reward Learning, a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach, where connected agents share experience fragments to improve training efficiency. By exchanging knowledge in real-time, they collectively develop a better understanding of their environment, increasing the effectiveness of their collaboration. We demonstrate the potential of this technique through two multi-agent applications: a simple target tracking task and a complex robotic swarm attack simulation. In the initial scenario, the performance of MSRL outshines MARL in all tested scenarios, highlighting the benefits of a reward-based learning approach. Furthermore, MSRL effectively adapts to changing environmental dynamics in the target tracking task. In the second scenario, the results show that MSRL can efficiently handle high-dimensional state observations. We believe that this research paves the way for future studies exploring the benefits of reward learning in multi-agent reinforcement learning environments. In machine learning, discrete stochasticness plays a significant role in tasks such as selecting model parameters, building neural network architectures, and performing optimization with discrete variables. Sampling from these discrete distributions holds great value, but it's challenging due to their intractability. This review delves into the widely applied Gumbel-softmax technique and its extensions like Gumble-Svante and SoftGMM, which enable efficient sampling and approximation of discrete distributions. These methods employ the principle that the ratio of densities for continuous random variables mapped to the unit simplex are independent and follow the Gumbel distribution. Building upon this concept, the review covers various applications, including variational autoencoders, generative models, and sequence generation. It also highlights the issues associated with negative log-likelihood and offers potential solutions, while discussing the role of softness in discrete stochastic processes. However, these datasets often have limited scope, making them unsuitable for real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach that leverages multiple smaller datasets to achieve state-of-the-art performance comparable to the largest datasets available. Specifically, we propose the use of a teacher-student framework, where a primary model is trained on a larger dataset while a secondary model is trained on a smaller dataset. By incorporating an additional module that combines the predictions of both models, we can effectively transfer knowledge from the primary model to augment the performance of the secondary model. This approach is demonstrated to be effective through a series of experiments on the MOT17 tracking benchmark, utilizing a combination of four datasets. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing top-tier methods, while also showcasing improved robustness against class imbalances. Furthermore, we make our code and trained models publicly available to facilitate future advancements in object detection. Open information extraction, which extracts individual facts from large text collections, has been a significant challenge in the field of information extraction. By incorporating a graph-based approach, Graphene is able to capture the nuances of complex sentences and related concepts, which in turn leads to improved accuracy in and coverage of open extraction. Molecular simulations typically rely on sampling methods that use the energy terrain's landscape to understand a system's behavior. However, when dealing with complex systems, direct evaluation can be computationally expensive, resulting in inaccurate free energy estimates. To address this, an alternative method is to use an approximate free energy terrain that can be explored more efficiently. We propose a new approach, adaptive reinforced dynamics, which combines a biased dynamics engine with continuous learning. This approach enables the calculation of free energies and the application of this method to various biochemical systems, such as protein folding and solvation, and tautomerization reactions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that this method can efficiently explore complex free energy landscapes, even those with multiple minima, in just a few iterations. With its ability to learn and adapt, our approach can reduce the need for complex terrain landscapes, making it a valuable tool in molecular simulations. We propose a novel approach that incorporates a trainable threshold for determining the accuracy of PINN predictions, and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments in both spatially distributed and time-dependent ODE problems. Our results show that this method effectively identifies overconfident predictions and achieves comparable or superior performance compared to existing evaluation techniques. Furthermore, we highlight the potential limitations of this method and offer potential avenues for future research in this area. The code and datasets used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. The findings of this work are expected to facilitate the development of more reliable and accurate PINN solutions for solving ODE problems. High-quality video conferencing demands nearly lossless video quality, creating a challenge of managing video bitrates, particularly on low-quality networks. Typically, bitrate control methods involve reducing video quality by degrading resolution, which compromises aesthetics. Our solution, Gemino, employs an innovative neural-based approach that compresses video streams after being transmitted, utilizing a lightweight neural model to restore video quality without affecting bitrate. Gemino's novel architecture, combining both spatial and temporal components, enables efficient video enhancement while minimizing computational requirements. Furthermore, Gemino's design allows for parallel processing, enabling high performance on multi-core GPUs. Our evaluation of Gemino in popular conferencing tools shows significant improvements in visual quality, with bitrates reduced by 25-50% compared to baseline results. Furthermore, Gemino's ability to handle packet loss and diverse network conditions was successfully demonstrated. Our implementation, based on the popular conferencing tool WebRTC, is available for public use. This project serves as an example of practical, resilient video compression that meets the needs of real-world conferencing applications.

This research tackles the complex challenge of attires that can be manipulated multiple times. To address this issue, we have developed a novel framework that utilizes a unique combination of image alignment and standardization. The proposed framework consists of three key stages: attire detection, alignment, and standardization. The first stage identifies the human body pose from the input image using a pose estimation technique. Subsequently, the attire manipulation stage aligns the human and attire regions based on their spatial relationship. The final stage, canonicalization, transforms the image into a standard template by fitting it to a predefined attire form. The outcome of this process is a standard image that can be used for multiple purposes, such as image editing, generation, and segmentation. The proposed framework has been tested on multiple tasks, including image editing, generation, segmentation, and manipulation, and has demonstrated its effectiveness in outperforming existing methods. The resilience of deep learning models in adversarial conditions has long been a concern, often resulting in decreased accuracy when subjected to intentional distortions. In robotics, this issue is particularly pronounced due to the inherent risks and costs associated with physical interactions. This study explores the relationship between the accuracy and adversarial resilience of reinforcement learning agents trained to perform a complex reaching task, and reveals that these two quantities are more interconnected than previously thought. Moreover, we found that the accuracy and adversarial resilience of these agents can be significantly enhanced simultaneously without sacrificing performance in clean environments, and that this improvement is achievable through the use of reinforcement learning alone. Our results suggest that this inherent trade-off is not present in robot learning, and that agents trained using reinforcement learning exhibit better robustness and accuracy than their supervised learning counterparts. Additionally, we found that the accuracy and adversarial resilience of these agents can be improved by incorporating data augmentation techniques, such as data mixing, into the training process. This study contributes to the field by providing new insights into the relationship between accuracy and adversarial resilience, and by demonstrating the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in achieving robust and accurate models, even without adversarial data augmentation. Our results also highlight the importance of considering both clean and adversarial data in robot learning, and the need for a more comprehensive approach to building resilient robot learning agents. This study paves the way for future research into the robustness and accuracy of deep learning models in robot learning, and the development of more resilient and accurate agents. The field of open-set identification addresses the challenge of recognizing when an input falls outside known classes. This issue is significant in real-world scenarios where data often contains unknown or novel instances. Most existing approaches to open-set identification are based on the premise that training and testing data share the same distribution. However, when the distribution changes between training and testing phases, these methods often struggle to detect out-of-distribution inputs. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages similarity learning to develop a more robust open-set identification method. Our approach involves generating diverse, synthetic examples from a single input and then learning a similarity function that distinguishes in-distribution from out-of-distribution data. This novel method is capable of adapting to changing data distributions and performing well across a wide range of scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and MNIST. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both accuracy and robustness to distribution shifts. We also provide code for our method on https://github.com/zhzytex/os-i. Additionally, we release a new benchmark for open-set identification and report our results, along with those of other leading methods. The benchmark can be found at https://os-benchmark.github.io. We hope that our contributions will inspire further research in this area. This work is accepted for publication in the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2022).
